catalog_quote: Stress has been derived in this grammar with a lexical rule determining root stress and various suffixes being introduced either with or without stress. Stress is distinguished by high tone and lack of stress with regular tone. (1) Root Stress (Obligatory) The root stress rule has word-final long vowels stressed, roots with final short vowels taking penultimate stress, and consonant-final roots taking stress on the last syllable. The few exceptions must be listed lexically. ... This rule avoids marking stress on nouns in the lexicon by listing the stressed final vowel as long in the feminine class. Under this analysis, final long forms (feminine) and consonant-final (masculine) nouns have the last syllable stressed, while masculine nouns with short final vowels have penultimate stress. ... sweep_summary: Afar (afar1241) is in the catalog as set by morphology on Bliese 1981 §11.2.1. Four title-works with stress in the title resolve to three works. (1) Möhlig 1981 (SELAF 'Tons et accents' volume, pp.1-38) is not an Afar source: Glottolog's own record says the Afar code is a 'computerized assignment from "adequate"', the volume's contributors are all Bantu/Adamawa/Comorian specialists, and a Google Books full-text control finds the volume for 'bantou' but not for 'afar' or 'couchitique' — priority none. (2) Hayward 1991 (already held by the project from our reading of 9/16, re-read this search of works with stress in the title, quoted pp.117-131) is the only dedicated Afar accent study and refines the classification: same penult-vs-final gender/case-conditioned distribution as Bliese, but analysed as tonal accent with a single phrasal H on the first word of an NP/PP (last three syllables) — consistent with the standing 'retain set by morphology, add caution' ruling. (3) Morin 2005 (two Glottolog records for one Peeters book) is discourse-level text prosody ('espaces séquencés' per Banti's 2018 obituary and the publisher blurb), not a word-accent description; no open copy exists (Google Books no pages, HathiTrust/archive.org none, Peeters DB down) — print only, low priority. One new open first-hand source was found and read: Simeone-Senelle 2021 (LACITO, HAL, CC BY-NC-ND), which states a distinctive pitch accent whose predictable position on the penult or final marks gender and case — confirms the catalog. Nothing read contradicts the catalog; the deciding source (Bliese 1981) is not superseded. Google Books API and OpenAlex quotas were also exhausted, so lookups used Glottolog JSON, HAL, OpenLibrary, HathiTrust API, SUDOC SRU, the Google Books feeds endpoint and Aethiopica.

new_statements.quote: p.117: 'the Qafar-Saho languages display tonal accent rather than stress accent'. p.119: 'However many words there are in a NP (or PP), high tone is only associated with one syllable, and this is always located in the first word of the phrase. Furthermore, within this first word, high tone can only ever be associated with one of the last three syllables.' p.120: '5. High Tone Association (NPs and PPs) If the first word contains an accented syllable, H will associate with that syllable. Otherwise, H will associate with the final syllable of the first word.'

new_statements.reading: The one dedicated accent study of Afar. Prominence is a single high tone per NP/PP, on the phrase's first word, restricted to one of that word's last three syllables; within the word it lands on the lexically accented syllable (penult, in masculine nouns) and otherwise on the final syllable by default (all feminine V-final nouns, unaccented C-final masculines, loans). Nominative/genitive shift to final H = accent suppression. This is the same penult-vs-final, gender/case-conditioned distribution Bliese 1981 states as word stress, so the catalog's set by morphology position rule is confirmed in substance; the refinement is Hayward's explicit classification as tonal (pitch) accent rather than stress, with a phrasal association domain. The newly downloaded open source Simeone-Senelle 2021 (p.32: 'accent de hauteur distinctif, dont la place, prédictible, marque le genre, le cas'; accent on penult or final) independently confirms the same facts and is the best NEW open first-hand statement, but is a genitive/compounding paper rather than an accent study.

sources.note: The only dedicated study of Afar (Qafar) accent. Prominence = a single phrasal high tone on the first word of an NP/PP, on one of that word's last three syllables; its syllable is fixed by lexical accent if present, else default final. Reanalysis (p.125, table 14): lexically accented nouns = C-final or V-final with penult H (all masculine); unaccented = C-final nouns with final H and all V-final feminine nouns (final H by default). p.126: nominative/genitive shift to final H analysed as accentual suppression. p.131: 'if a lexical noun ends in a consonant and/or carries accent, it is masculine…

sources.quote: p.32: 'Il existe un accent de hauteur distinctif, dont la place, prédictible, marque le genre, le cas (pour les noms soumis à la flexion), et permet aussi de distinguer entre une unité syntagmatique et une unité lexématique.' p.33: 'Le syntagme est composé de deux lexèmes, deux unités accentuelles, chacune gardant son sens lexical plein. La première est toujours accentuée sur la pénultième ou la finale'. p.34: 'il y a apophonie de la voyelle finale et déplacement de l'accent sur cette finale : -a# / -u# > -í#.' p.44: 'l'accent affecte la syllabe finale ou pénultième.' [EN: There is a distinctive pitch accent whose predictable position marks gender, case (for inflected nouns), and distinguishes a phrase from a lexeme ... The first is always accented on the penult or the final ... the accent affects the final or penultimate syllable.]
sources.note: First-hand (LACITO/CNRS fieldworker, native co-editors), open. Each Afar noun carries one accent, on the penult or the final; position is predictable and encodes gender and case (nominative/genitive of masculine -a/-u nouns: final-vowel apophony to -í with accent shift to the final; masculine -i-final and penult-accented trisyllabic C-final nouns mark genitive by accent shift to the final, p.34); a lexicalised compound has a single accent 'soumise aux mêmes règles accentuelles que le nom simple' (p.44). Calls it 'accent de hauteur' (pitch accent) on p.32 but 'accent d'intensité' with measured…
